knowledge.pageSubtitle: Answers for your medical trip to Thailand
knowledge.disclaimer: This is general information to help you prepare — not medical, immigration, or binding insurance advice. Please confirm details with the hospital or clinic, immigration checkpoint, or your insurer before you travel.

lao-cross-border-treatment.title: Can Lao citizens get treatment in Thailand?
lao-cross-border-treatment.teaser: A quick answer on the documents and steps to know before crossing over for care

sections.heading: In general, yes
sections.body: Most private hospitals and clinics in Thailand accept self-paying foreign patients regardless of nationality. You'll need a valid passport plus a border pass or visa for the checkpoint you're using — requirements can vary depending on how long you plan to stay and which crossing you use.

sections.heading: Documents you'll usually need
sections.body: A passport valid for several more months, the border pass or visa required for your entry point, the destination hospital's contact details, and — if you've been treated before — a translated copy of your medical records in case the doctor needs to reference them.

sections.heading: What to confirm with the hospital beforehand
sections.body: Call or message ahead to ask whether they have a foreign-patient coordination team or a Lao-Thai interpreter, what payment methods they accept, and if your condition is more complex, book an appointment in advance so a specialist is available.

insurance-coverage.title: Does my health insurance work at Thai hospitals?
insurance-coverage.teaser: Coverage varies by policy — here's what to check before you travel

sections.heading: Your domestic health insurance
sections.body: Most national or domestic health insurance plans only cover treatment received within your own country. Care at a Thai hospital usually isn't covered unless your policy explicitly states it includes cross-border treatment.

sections.heading: Travel or international health insurance
sections.body: Some travel or international health insurance plans cover emergency treatment abroad. Check whether pre-existing conditions are covered, and whether the plan covers planned (non-emergency) treatment as well as emergencies.

sections.heading: Pay first, claim later
sections.body: Many patients pay the Thai hospital directly, then submit receipts and a medical report to their insurer for reimbursement afterward. Ask your insurer in advance exactly which documents they need, and whether those documents need to be translated.

clinic-vs-hospital.title: What's the difference between a clinic and a hospital?
clinic-vs-hospital.teaser: Understand the difference so you can pick the right place for your needs

sections.heading: Size and scope of care
sections.body: Clinics are typically small and focused on a specific specialty — dental, dermatology, or minor procedures that don't require an overnight stay — with shorter wait times. Hospitals are larger, cover many departments, and can handle surgery, inpatient stays, and complex or emergency cases.

sections.heading: Which one fits your situation
sections.body: For routine checkups, dental work, or minor cosmetic procedures, a clinic is usually faster and works well. For surgery, hospital admission, complex diagnostics, or an emergency, a hospital is the safer choice.

sections.heading: Cost and time
sections.body: Clinics tend to be cheaper and quicker for straightforward cases. Hospitals may charge additional facility fees, but offer more backup and continuity of care if complications come up.
